question_types.description: Player sees one full email and chooses Phishing or Legitimate.

scenario.subject: Reminder: Grade Encoding Period Ends Friday
scenario.body: Hi students, this is a reminder that the grade encoding period for this semester closes this Friday at 5 PM. If you notice a missing grade after that, visit the Registrar's window in person. No action is needed from you right now.

questions.tell: Real school domain, no link, no request for personal info, and no urgency trick.
questions.correct_feedback: Nice catch — a plain notice with no ask is usually safe.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Check the sender's domain and what it actually asks you to do — nothing here.
questions.explanation: The address matches the real school domain and the email doesn't ask you to click, download, or share anything. It's just information.

scenario.subject: URGENT: Wifi Access Expiring Today
scenario.body: Your campus wifi account will be disabled in 2 hours. Re-enter your student ID and password now to keep your access: westfie1d.edu/wifi-fix

questions.tell: The domain uses the numeral 1 instead of the letter l — westfie1d.edu, not westfield.edu.
questions.correct_feedback: Exactly — that's a lookalike domain built to fool a quick glance.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Look closely at the domain spelling — one letter is swapped for a number.
questions.explanation: Real wifi accounts don't get disabled with a 2-hour countdown, and no legitimate IT team asks you to type your password into a link like this. The domain is also a lookalike.

scenario.subject: Overdue Fine Notice - ₱350
scenario.body: You have an unpaid library fine of ₱350. Open the attached FINE_NOTICE.PDF.exe and log in with your student credentials today to avoid a hold on your enrollment.

questions.tell: The attachment is disguised as a PDF but ends in .exe, a program file, not a document.
questions.correct_feedback: Right — a real fine notice is never a program pretending to be a PDF.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Look at the attachment name closely — it isn't really a PDF.
questions.explanation: The .PDF.exe extension is a classic disguise for a malicious program. Combined with an outside domain and a credential login request, this is a clear phishing attempt.

scenario.subject: Club Fair Booth Sign-Up Closes Monday
scenario.body: If your organization wants a booth at next month's club fair, submit the sign-up form at the Student Activities office by Monday. Questions can be directed to our office during business hours.

questions.tell: Real domain, no link to click, and the action happens in person, not online.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — informational, real domain, nothing risky requested.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Re-check the sender address and what action is actually being asked for.
questions.explanation: This email matches the real school domain and asks students to submit a form in person rather than click a link or share credentials.

scenario.subject: Confirm Your Enrollment Record
scenario.body: Reply to this email with your full student number and portal password so we can confirm your enrollment record before the deadline tomorrow.

questions.tell: The display name says Registrar's Office, but the actual address is a free gmail.com account.
questions.correct_feedback: Exactly — a real office never emails from a personal gmail account.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Look past the display name — check the actual email address after the @.
questions.explanation: A legitimate registrar's office uses the official school domain, not a personal gmail address. Asking you to reply with your password by email is also a hard red flag.

scenario.subject: Scheduled Maintenance This Saturday
scenario.body: The student portal will be briefly unavailable this Saturday from 1 AM to 3 AM for scheduled maintenance. No action is required. Service will resume automatically.

questions.tell: Real domain, calm tone, and explicitly says no action is required.
questions.correct_feedback: Right — no ask, no urgency, real domain.
questions.incorrect_feedback: This email doesn't ask you to do anything at all — that's a good sign, not a bad one.
questions.explanation: This is a routine maintenance notice from the correct school domain. It doesn't request any action, which is typical of legitimate IT announcements.

scenario.subject: Claim Your ₱1,500 Student Stipend - Expires in 24 Hours
scenario.body: You've been selected for a ₱1,500 student stipend. Click below to claim it before your slot expires in 24 hours: northline-credit.com/claim-stipend. You will need to confirm your account number and PIN.

questions.tell: The real credit union uses northlinecu.edu, not northline-credit.com, and no legitimate stipend program asks for your PIN.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — free money plus a countdown plus a PIN request is a classic combo.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Would a real stipend program ever need your account PIN to give you money? That's the tell.
questions.explanation: This message stacks three tricks: an unexpected reward, a false deadline, and a request for sensitive account details on an unfamiliar domain.

scenario.subject: Your Checkup Reminder for Next Week
scenario.body: This is a reminder of your scheduled checkup next Tuesday at 10 AM. To reschedule, call the clinic front desk at the number on your student ID. No online action is needed.

questions.tell: Real domain and the only requested action is a phone call, not a link or login.
questions.correct_feedback: Nice — a real domain and an offline way to respond.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Notice there's no link and no request for a password — that points to legitimate.
questions.explanation: The domain matches the school, and rescheduling happens by phone rather than through a link or login, which fits normal clinic communication.

scenario.subject: Sharing Error on 'Class 10 Notes' Folder
scenario.body: A sharing error occurred on your class folder. Sign in here with your school email and password to restore access: drive-share-alert.com/fix-access

questions.tell: The domain has nothing to do with the school or a known drive provider, and it asks for your school password on that outside site.
questions.correct_feedback: Correct — an unrelated domain asking for your school password is a big red flag.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Check where the sign-in link actually points — is that domain connected to your school at all?
questions.explanation: Legitimate shared drive tools don't route password logins through unrelated third-party domains. This is built to steal your school credentials.

scenario.subject: Unusual Sign-In Detected - Account Will Be Locked
scenario.body: We detected a sign-in from a new device. If this wasn't you, your account will be permanently locked in 1 hour unless you verify your identity here: westfield-it-secure.net/verify. Enter your username and password to cancel the lock.

questions.tell: The real school domain is westfield.edu — 'westfield-it-secure.net' is a different, unrelated domain designed to look official.
questions.correct_feedback: Exactly — fear of a locked account is the pressure tactic here.
questions.incorrect_feedback: Compare this domain letter-by-letter with the real westfield.edu address.
questions.explanation: This combines a scary consequence (permanent lock), a tight deadline, and a lookalike domain that isn't the actual school domain — all designed to make you act before you think.

questions.question: What is the strongest sign this email is fake?
options: The subject line is in all caps
The domain has a 1 instead of an l
It was sent in the morning
questions.explanation: westfie1d.edu is a lookalike of the real westfield.edu domain — that's the strongest tell here.

scenario.subject: Pay Now to Avoid Hold

questions.question: What is the strongest sign this email is fake?
options: The attachment is disguised as a PDF but is really a program (.exe)
questions.explanation: A file ending in .PDF.exe is actually an executable program, not a document — a common malware disguise.

questions.explanation: The urgency plus the password request plus the lookalike domain together are the tell, but the domain and password ask are the core issue.

It comes from the student council
questions.explanation: westfield.edu.form-reply.com is not a subdomain of westfield.edu — the real domain is form-reply.com, with 'westfield.edu' added to trick the eye.

questions.text: A file named 'notice.PDF.exe' is a real PDF document.
questions.explanation: The .exe ending means it's a program, not a document, no matter what comes before it.

questions.text: Urgent deadlines and threats of account lockout are common pressure tactics in phishing emails.
questions.explanation: Creating panic makes people act before they think carefully — a common phishing tactic.

questions.text: It's safer to type a known website address yourself than to click a link in an unexpected email.
questions.explanation: Typing the address yourself avoids lookalike domains hidden behind a clickable link.

questions.text: A domain like 'westfie1d.edu' is exactly the same as 'westfield.edu'.
questions.explanation: Swapping a letter for a similar-looking number creates a completely different, unrelated domain.

questions.text: If an email offers unexpected free money or a reward, it's worth being extra cautious.
questions.explanation: Unexpected rewards are a common lure used to get people to click links or share information.

questions.text: Reporting a suspicious email is only useful if you're completely certain it's phishing.
questions.explanation: It's fine to report anything suspicious — school IT or admins can verify it, even if you're unsure.

questions.text: An email that asks you to reply with your ID number and birthdate to 'claim a grant' is safe as long as it mentions a real-sounding organization.
questions.explanation: Mentioning a real-sounding name doesn't verify the sender — the domain and the request itself matter more.

questions.text: A calm email from your school's real domain that asks for no action and no personal information is generally safe to read.
questions.explanation: Legitimate, informational emails from a verified domain that request nothing risky are normal and safe.
